scenes.heading: Poetry and visual texts
scenes.sub: Reading the shape, sound and pictures of a text
scenes.say: Poems and posters say a lot in very few words. To read them well, you need to notice their shape, their sounds and their pictures, not just their sentences.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A song's beat and tune add feeling the lyrics alone can't
scenes.science: A poem's rhythm, line breaks and images add meaning
scenes.breaks: you hear a song's tune; with a poem on paper you must hear the rhythm in your head.
scenes.say: Think of a song. The beat and the tune add feeling that the words alone can't. A poem is the same: its rhythm, line breaks and images add meaning. But on paper there's no music, so read it in your head and listen.

scenes.heading: Poetry toolkit
points: Theme: the big idea about life
scenes.say: Here's your poetry toolkit. A simile compares using like or as. Personification makes a thing act like a person. Rhyme, rhythm and line breaks shape how it sounds. Mood is the feeling it creates, and theme is the big idea.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: 'Its tin roof sighs when the north wind blows.' Which technique, and what effect?
lines: A human action for a thing
Effect: the shed seems old, tired
scenes.say: Its tin roof sighs when the north wind blows. Can a roof really sigh? No. Giving a human action to a thing is personification. The effect is that the shed seems old and tired, like a person.

scenes.heading: Reading a visual text
steps: What do I see first, and why?
What do words and image say together?
What does it want me to do?
scenes.say: For posters, cartoons and infographics, ask four questions. What do I see first, and why? What do the words and picture say together? Who is it for? And what does it want me to do or think?

scenes.heading: Cartoon irony

left.title: The words say
points: Sign on the wall: Family Time

right.title: The picture shows
points: The dog waiting for a walk

scenes.say: Cartoons often use irony. In our cartoon, a sign says family time, but everyone is staring at their own phone and the dog is ignored. When the words and the picture disagree, that clash is the message.

points: Name the tool, then its effect
The ending often holds the meaning
scenes.say: Quick recap. Read a poem twice, once for meaning and once for tools. Name each tool and its effect. Check the ending. In visual texts, the biggest, brightest thing carries the main message. Now try the practice questions!
